rationale: EASE LID 2 follows 223 participants receiving open-label extended-release amantadine for Parkinson dyskinesia. Hallucination adverse events and time to onset were tracked; the common named event was reported in 24.2% of participants. The extension re-enrolled participants from earlier trials and also enrolled a deep-brain-stimulation cohort. NCT02202551 is a medication safety study without a dried fig exposure or controlled food comparison.

An autopsy case links a clinical Lewy body dementia course to neuropathology. Occasional visual hallucinations were reported before donepezil treatment and were described as resolving after treatment in this patient. The longitudinal case gives medication and pathology context and documents neither dried fig ingestion nor a food-related episode rate.

A Parkinson cohort was followed after bilateral subthalamic stimulation. The sleep scale includes an item for distressing nighttime hallucinations, which differs from all-day visual episode counts. Stimulation follow-up and medication context provide no comparison by dried fig intake.

OPTIPARK is an open-label opicapone safety and effectiveness study for motor fluctuations. Visual hallucination appears among serious events considered possibly treatment related. Seven of 495 participants had one or more of the listed related serious events, a grouped figure that cannot be assigned to visual hallucination alone. The study intervention was opicapone and there is no dried fig exposure.

The case concerns central and peripheral neurological signs during severe SARS-CoV-2 infection. The discussion names psychiatric symptoms among broader possible neurological phenotypes. Acute infection and critical illness are distinct from Parkinson visual hallucination frequency after a culinary exposure.

DUPARC specifies vision and other nonmotor phenotyping in de novo Parkinson disease and planned a three-day dietary diary for nutrient intake. It also identifies diet as a potential confounder in the microbiome analysis. The protocol reports no separate dried fig measure, fig comparison or exposure-linked visual hallucination outcome. Registry NCT04180865 identifies this cohort.

Parkinson groups with and without psychotic symptoms were compared using an emotional salience task and neuroimaging. The phenotype includes visual hallucinations, delusions or illusions. Group classification and stimulus processing were examined without a fig exposure or diet-linked count of visual episodes.

This case describes writing-specific impairment and recurrent clinical visual hallucinations in probable Lewy body dementia. Diagnostic imaging and the course of symptoms inform the differential diagnosis. No dried fig exposure or food comparison was reported.

The investigators studied genetic findings in early-onset Parkinson disease. Visual hallucinations appear as a clinical phenotype abbreviation in the cohort record. Exposure, timing and response to dried figs are outside the genotyping comparison.

The study compares eye fixations and presaccadic potentials during an ambiguous visual task. Pareidolias are responses to stimuli, measured under test conditions. That comparison gives perceptual context but does not measure changes in spontaneous visual hallucination frequency after eating dried figs.

Clinical visual hallucinator groups were compared using structural brain-network controllability and regional gene-expression maps. The imaging group associations do not quantify an exposure-linked episode rate. No dried fig intervention or measured intake informed this analysis.

This clinical audit follows opicapone use in people who previously had insufficient benefit from entacapone or could not tolerate it. The report tabulates treatment-emergent hallucinations and discusses psychosis in the context of dopaminergic medication. It supplies no evidence involving dried fig exposure or a Parkinson episode-rate comparison by diet.

The single-center genetic counseling series applies a familial dementia protocol. A selected phenotype description includes a visual-hallucination episode amid other psychiatric symptoms. The analytic comparison is genetic and diagnostic and supplies no dried fig exposure.

A rapidly progressive Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease case developed visual hallucinations along with cognitive and motor changes. The study measures an electrophysiological cortical silent period. This disease and procedure context gives no dried fig exposure or Parkinson episode-rate outcome.

A small multimodal imaging study uses synaptic PET in Lewy body dementia. Visual hallucinations are recorded in clinical characterization of participants. The study compares imaging measures rather than documented dietary exposure or change in hallucination frequency.

The Parkinson study measured visual performance, cognition and white matter. Clinical hallucination presence and a separate severity questionnaire were recorded at baseline. Neither those measures nor later cognitive change was compared by dried fig intake.

The case traces cognitive and behavioral change in pathology-confirmed vascular parkinsonism. Possible visual hallucination or illusion appears in the history with medication and disease progression. No dried fig intake was measured and the uncertain case phenotype does not supply a comparison.

The report documents a posterior cortical atrophy phenotype in a GBA variant carrier. Overt visual hallucinations were absent during the reported follow-up despite visuospatial difficulties and mild parkinsonian features. The negative observation describes the phenotype and has no dried fig exposure.

The Parkinson imaging study relates structural and functional connectivity to network organization and neuromodulatory profiles. Hallucinations appear in clinical motivation and interpretation. The measures do not quantify a hallucination response to dried figs.

The qualitative study interviewed care partners about lived experience of Parkinson psychosis and reports multiple hallucination modalities. The interview data provide symptom and caregiving context. They supply neither a dried fig comparison nor a prospective count of visual episodes by diet.

The pooled post hoc analysis uses EASE LID and EASE LID 3 data, NCT02136914 and NCT02274766. At week 12 the MDS-UPDRS hallucinations and psychosis item was 0.2 points higher after Gocovri than after placebo in the adjusted analysis (P < 0.001). The scored item combines experiences and cannot be treated as an independent food effect or a count of visual episodes. This analysis overlaps the parent randomized trial populations, which also contributed extension participants.

The imaging comparison studies interhemispheric connectivity and impulse-control disorders in Parkinson disease. Severe visual hallucinations interfering with assessment were an exclusion criterion. The study did not measure a hallucination response to dried figs.

A Parkinson registry analysis compares reported double vision and associated patient characteristics. The nonmotor questionnaire asks about auditory or visual hallucinations as a combined presence outcome. Its observed association with diplopia does not identify diet, dried figs or frequency after exposure.

The report uses neuropsychiatric and neuropsychological assessment for a frontotemporal dementia case. Hallucinations appear in the clinical narrative and assessment domains. It provides no dried fig exposure or Parkinson-specific comparison.

People with Parkinson disease performed an illusory-contour task alongside a cortical metabolism analysis. No patient reported visual hallucinations during the preceding month under the study assessment. Task performance and the baseline restriction do not test dried figs or change in episode frequency.

The comparison uses face pareidolia and associated frontotemporal connectivity in Parkinson disease. Mistaking ambiguous stimuli for faces is the controlled task. This differs from spontaneous recurrence and does not compare dried fig intake.

The skin-biopsy study compares synuclein findings in Parkinson disease and atypical syndromes. A case description reports emergent visual hallucinations after levodopa. The reported drug timing and pathology provide no dried fig exposure or food-linked visual episode count.

The secondary analysis groups motor and nonmotor Parkinson features into symptom sets. Visual hallucinations appear in a modeled symptom cluster. Cluster membership and estimated symptom probabilities do not constitute dietary exposure or change in observed episode frequency.

The case describes intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with rapidly progressive dementia and stroke. Visual and auditory hallucinations were not reported in that patient's course. The comparison is diagnostic and contains no relevant food exposure.

The Parkinson study compares retinal structure using optical coherence tomography and discusses visual complaints. Retinal dimensions and vision findings are distinct from a measured visual hallucination rate by food exposure. Dried fig use was not studied.

The study validates a subjective cognitive complaints instrument in Parkinson disease. It uses the timing of cognitive impairment or hallucinations in exclusions designed to distinguish Lewy body dementia. The criteria do not supply an episode rate or dietary exposure.

The ophthalmology study records a range of eye disorders and visual symptoms in Parkinson disease, including hallucination reports. These presentation data do not measure changes after dried fig consumption or compare people by fig exposure.

The postmortem study analyzes a microglial regulatory ligand and receptor in Parkinson brain tissue. Hallucinations appear in clinical metadata and mechanistic discussion. Protein expression groups do not measure dried fig intake or a symptom rate after ingestion.

The study measures poly(ADP-ribose) and alpha-synuclein in extracellular vesicles and relates levels to clinical severity. Four of 20 people in the discovery group had evidence of visual hallucinations. Grouping clinical manifestations by disease severity does not measure a response to dried figs.

A pathology-confirmed corticobasal degeneration case showed REM sleep behavior disorder and visual hallucinations. The case challenges a simple inference from hallucination phenotype to synuclein pathology. It supplies no dried fig exposure or dietary contrast in Parkinson disease.

The retrospective deep-brain-stimulation analysis relates lead topography and depression history to neuropsychological outcomes. A history of visual illusion or hallucination outside delirium was a clinical characteristic. The exposure is surgical and there is no dried fig use or food-linked frequency estimate.

The Parkinson imaging and motor-task study tests microstructural associations with bimanual control. Visual hallucinations are mentioned as findings in earlier cited tract studies. This original contributes no exposure measurement or new episode-rate estimate for dried figs.

The case describes unusual sleep behavior, rapid ataxia, cognitive decline and visual hallucinations during a progressive neurological illness. It supplies a differential-diagnosis and temporal context. No dried fig intake or Parkinson food comparison was recorded.

The report describes reversible anomic aphasia and delirium after electroconvulsive therapy combined with lithium. Auditory and visual phenomena occurred during the acute treatment course. This case is not a Parkinson culinary exposure comparison and has no dried fig evidence.

The study compares fecal microbial profiles across Lewy body dementia, Parkinson disease, isolated REM sleep behavior disorder and control groups. Visual hallucinations characterize the dementia syndrome in the introduction. The reported models compare microbial communities and recorded covariates, with no itemized dried fig exposure or hallucination rate linked to intake.

A prospective Parkinson analysis evaluates baseline visual hallucinations and subjective cognitive complaints as predictors of later cognition. The NMSS perception domain records frequency and severity over the prior four weeks. The modeled outcome is cognitive impairment during follow-up and the study does not compare dried fig intake.

The case follows posture and gait changes, later cognitive symptoms and visual hallucinations in anti-IgLON5 disease. The diagnostic workup provides a parkinsonism differential. There is no dried fig exposure or food-linked visual hallucination frequency measurement.

APOKADO compares home and hospital initiation of continuous subcutaneous apomorphine for Parkinson disease. Follow-up describes hallucination severity and time points under treatment. Treatment setting and medication exposure cannot resolve the dried fig hypothesis.

The study compares macular capillary plexus and ganglion cell complex measurements in Parkinson disease. Visual hallucinations appear in the background on visual dysfunction. The imaging analysis tests neither dried figs nor a change in spontaneous episode frequency.

ANNES is a pilot protocol for drug neuroenhancement in intensive or intermediate care, NCT05479032. It describes hallucinations as a safety condition for reducing study medication. Planned dose management in critically ill patients gives no result for a Parkinson food exposure.
